first_impression.reaction: James's mum is Mexican-Australian and his abuela keeps asking who our padrinos will be, so I Googled it. The intro is calm and grown-up: 'A Mexican wedding belongs to the whole family' is exactly the conversation we're having at home, and it promised the day in order plus the Australian bit at the end. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Parents, grandparents and godparents play a part long before the ceremony, and sponsors carry the objects that make the Mass their own.
journey.reaction: No 'fairytale', no 'dream day'. It tells me straight away this is a family production, not just the two of us. Good.

journey.quote: In Mexico the civil ceremony is the legal marriage, and a church wedding does not replace it, so couples who want a Mass plan both.
journey.reaction: This is the single most useful line for us. I'd have assumed the church wedding counted. Two ceremonies changes the whole guest schedule.

journey.section: 1. Before the wedding: la pedida de mano and the serenata
journey.quote: A study of weddings in Almoloya del Río, in the State of Mexico, describes three moments of the pedimento de mano, the aviso, the acuerdo and the contento, which have changed in their details but not in essence for at least two centuries.
journey.reaction: Interesting, but sections 1 and 2 are very anthropological: Nahua, Totonac, Almoloya del Río. I started skimming for the bits that tell me what to actually do. The line about building the pedida visits into the months before we set a date pulled me back.

journey.quote: Hold that conversation early, and never assume what someone will offer.
journey.reaction: Honest and practical. Money with James's family is exactly the awkward talk we're avoiding, and this tells me to have it now.

journey.quote: In the families the study describes, the padrinos de lazo must be a stable couple married in the church, as an example to their godchildren.
journey.reaction: That's the kind of detail that would cause a family incident if we got it wrong. Plus 'Brief your photographer: the moment comes quickly.' Insider stuff.

journey.quote: Your parish priest will guide the order of service. Give each sponsor their cue and seat in writing.
journey.reaction: Clear. With six or seven sets of padrinos I can see why a written run sheet matters. Who writes it, though? Us or you?

journey.quote: The custom is closely associated with Guanajuato and Zacatecas, where the state government has described a callejoneada as an icebreaker before the wedding ceremony, with guests touring the historic centre.
journey.reaction: Loved the idea, then hit section 13 and saw Guanajuato and Zacatecas are both on the 'Reconsider your need to travel' list. My parents would read those two sections together and panic. I'd want the article to join those dots for me, not leave me to.

journey.quote: When you book, ask how many musicians will come and whether trumpets are included.
journey.reaction: Useful, though the section is mostly history before it gets here. Again it's 'when you book', meaning me doing it.

journey.quote: Have two steady guests beside each chair.
journey.reaction: Ha. Very real. This is the sort of detail that makes me think someone has actually stood in that room.

journey.quote: It advises Australians to "Reconsider your need to travel" to Chiapas, Chihuahua, Colima, Guanajuato, Guerrero, Michoacán, north-western Durango, Sinaloa, Sonora, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas, each with listed exceptions.
journey.reaction: I'd rather know, and the dated advice feels honest. But there's nothing on what a Mexico wedding looks like for 80 guests: where they'd stay, how my grandparents get from the airport to the venue, who's on the ground if something goes wrong. 'Couples who marry in Mexico tend to choose places outside the higher-level states' is one line.

journey.quote: Before you book, put these questions to the Registro Civil where you will marry and to the Australian Embassy:
journey.reaction: The question list is genuinely good, and the Playa del Carmen example (four witnesses, medical certificate valid 15 days) is specific. But the legal side is the thing I most want someone else to sort.

journey.quote: Many Mexican-Australian couples marry in Australia, with the Mass, the lazo and the arras in their own parish and the mariachi, the víbora and the cookies at the reception.
journey.reaction: Realistically this might be us. It's only a short paragraph though. I'd want to know how a planner fits around a parish and a big family who'll want to run half the day.

journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact for venue, travel, vendors and guest rooms, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee and inclusions confirmed in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Answers two of my biggest worries: who's accountable, and currency surprises. Best line on the page for me.

journey.quote: You deal with the registry, the Embassy and your parish directly.
journey.reaction: Honest, I'll give you that. But it lands right after the line that won me over, and it's the exact bit I hoped you'd take off our plate. At least tell me what help you do give on paperwork.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned Mexican or Mexican-Australian weddings before? Is there a real one with a venue and date I can look at?
If we married in Mexico, where would 60 to 90 guests stay, and how would older relatives get from the airport to the venue?
Who writes the run sheet with all the padrinos' cues and seats: you, us, or the priest?
What help, if any, do you give with the CNI, apostilles and translations, even if we have to lodge them ourselves?
How do you handle a two-ceremony schedule (civil one day, Mass the next) for guests flying in?
What's the back-up if a hurricane hits a coastal wedding between June and November?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Mexican Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait headline. The article is more thoughtful than its title. (Noted only; I understand it's fixed.)

would_share_with: James's mum and abuela (padrinos, lazo, arras and Mass sections)
My parents (only the legal steps and 'Bringing Mexican traditions home', not the Smartraveller list)

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, regions or a wedding at home, a Wedded Advisor is happy to start the conversation.
cta_reaction.why: No hard sell, and the written AUD fee is a real plus. But there's no real wedding on this page, and I want proof you've worked with a Mexican family before. I'd read one or two more posts and look for that first.

top_3_changes: Link to a real Mexican or Mexican-Australian wedding from your pages, with venue and date, so I can see you've done this before.

Join the dots between the callejoneada (Guanajuato, Zacatecas) and the Smartraveller list, and add a few lines on what a Mexico wedding means for guests: where they stay, getting there, hurricane back-up.

Soften the 'You deal with the registry, the Embassy and your parish directly' moment by saying what the Wedded Advisor does do around paperwork and the run sheet, and expand 'Bringing Mexican traditions home' with how a planner works alongside the family and parish.
